applications.summary: acme-api is the order-intake and payment service behind the ACME storefront: it charges the customer through Stripe, persists the order to PostgreSQL, and publishes an order-created event to Kafka for the fulfilment worker to pick up.
responsibilities: Expose the order HTTP API: create, fetch and cancel (apps/api/app/routers/orders.py:13,22,31)
Take payment via Stripe before recording the order (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:28)
Persist orders to PostgreSQL through a repository (apps/api/app/repositories/order_repository.py:16)
Publish an OrderCreated event to Kafka for the worker (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:35)
Serve an unauthenticated liveness check at GET /health (apps/api/app/main.py:12)

applications.summary: @acme/web is the browser storefront: it fetches a customer's orders from acme-api and renders them, with client-side routes for a list view and a per-order view.
responsibilities: Bootstrap the React app into the DOM (apps/web/src/main.tsx:5)

applications.summary: acme-worker is the asynchronous fulfilment side of the order flow: it consumes order-created events from Kafka, hands them to Celery to generate an invoice and store it in S3, and hosts a (currently unwired) nightly reconciliation task.
responsibilities: Consume orders.created events from Kafka and hand them to Celery (apps/worker/worker/consumer.py:12)
Run the fulfil_order task: derive an invoice reference and store an invoice object in S3 (apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:18)
Store invoice objects in the acme-invoices S3 bucket (apps/worker/worker/storage.py:9)
Define a reconcile task against the payment provider, though it is a stub with no caller (apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:26)

applications.summary: acme-shared is the contract library imported by both acme-api and acme-worker: it defines the Order/OrderLine domain model and the Kafka event names/payloads so the two services agree on what an order and an order event look like.
responsibilities: Define the Order and OrderLine dataclasses (packages/shared/shared/models.py:9,16)

components.summary: The FastAPI application root: wires the app and health endpoint (apps/api/app/main.py:8), holds runtime configuration including two committed secrets (apps/api/app/config.py:6,9), and a raw psycopg2 helper with one unparameterized, currently unused query (apps/api/app/db.py:14).

The entire React storefront: DOM bootstrap (apps/web/src/main.tsx:5), routes (apps/web/src/App.tsx:8), the axios API client (apps/web/src/api/client.ts:13), and the order list component that also renders fetch errors as raw HTML (apps/web/src/components/OrderList.tsx:13).

A small, framework-free contract library: the Order/OrderLine dataclasses (packages/shared/shared/models.py:9,16) and the Kafka topic constants plus OrderCreated event dataclass (packages/shared/shared/events.py:5,11) that acme-api and acme-worker both import.

flows.narrative: GET /health is an unauthenticated liveness probe: it always returns a static {"status": "ok"} without touching Postgres, Redis, Kafka or any external system (apps/api/app/main.py:12-14). It decides nothing and changes nothing, but that also means a green health check does not prove the service can actually take an order — none of its real dependencies are exercised.

A client calls POST /orders with a JSON payload; the handler requires customer_id (400 if missing) but never reads or requires order lines, so it always builds an Order with an empty lines list (apps/api/app/routers/orders.py:23-27). OrderService.create then rejects any order with no lines (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:26-27), so every POST /orders call currently fails with an unhandled ValueError before Stripe is even charged. GET /orders/{id} returns 404 via the repository lookup (apps/api/app/routers/orders.py:16-18); DELETE /orders/{id} just echoes a canned 'cancelled' response without touching the database or issuing a refund (apps/api/app/routers/orders.py:32-34), so it never actually cancels anything.

Triggered when the Kafka consumer receives an orders.created message and calls fulfil_order.delay(order_id) (apps/worker/worker/consumer.py:13-16). The Celery task derives an MD5 digest of the order id and stores it as the body of an S3 object under invoices/{order_id}.pdf (apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:19-22, apps/worker/worker/storage.py:9-12) — a placeholder, not a real invoice document. It returns the string ORDER_SHIPPED, but nothing publishes that value anywhere, so no order status is ever updated and no downstream system is told the order shipped.

The reconcile Celery task is defined to run nightly reconciliation against the payment provider per its docstring (apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:26-27), but nothing in this repository calls it — no Celery beat schedule, no Kafka topic and no other caller exist. It takes a day string and immediately returns 0, so as shipped it is an unwired stub rather than an implemented process.

findings.reasoning: find_orders_by_customer builds SQL by '%' string-formatting an unsanitised customer_id directly into the query, unlike the sibling OrderRepository which uses parameterised placeholders (apps/api/app/repositories/order_repository.py:13,19). The function is not called anywhere else in the repository today, so it is currently dead code, but it is a live SQL-injection landmine that will fire the moment something wires it to a request.

request_shipment disables certificate verification on an outbound HTTPS call to the shipping partner that carries an order_id (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:41-42), exposing it to MITM tampering. Like the SQL-format issue, this method is not called from any router or task in the repository, so it is not on a live path today, but it is real vulnerable code, not a false match.

PAYMENT_API_SECRET is a hardcoded Stripe secret key committed to the repository, and it is actively used to authenticate every Stripe call (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:16,28), not just declared and unused. Anything committed to git must be treated as compromised and rotated.

DEBUG is hardcoded to True with no environment gate at all, and is fed straight into FastAPI's debug flag (apps/api/app/main.py:5,8), so every deployment — not just local dev — runs with FastAPI debug mode (stack traces, interactive tracebacks) on.

The application never reads a DEBUG environment variable — apps/api/app/config.py:5 hardcodes DEBUG = True as a literal, not via os.getenv — so ENV DEBUG=1 in the Dockerfile has no effect on runtime behaviour; it's dead configuration. The real, effective debug-mode bug is apps/api/app/config.py:5, already reported separately.

The error state is built from String(e) on whatever the axios request throws (apps/web/src/components/OrderList.tsx:10) and then injected as raw HTML instead of text (line 13). Nothing sanitises it, and there is no reason it needs to be HTML rather than a text node — even if today's failure strings look benign, any error message that ever echoes response content would execute as markup.

This MD5 use is not for authentication, integrity or password storage — it derives a placeholder reference string that becomes the body (not the key) of a stub S3 'invoice' object (apps/worker/worker/tasks.py:21-22, apps/worker/worker/storage.py:9-11). MD5's cryptographic weaknesses (collision/preimage attacks) are not a security concern for this non-security use, though the invoice content itself being a bare hash is a separate correctness/business concern.

The service is only ever run inside a container: the Dockerfile CMD also binds 0.0.0.0 (apps/api/Dockerfile:7) and docker-compose publishes the same port mapping (docker-compose.yml service api, port 8080:8080). Binding to all interfaces inside a container is required for the published port to work at all, not an extra exposure beyond what compose already does.

insights.title: Three biggest risks: committed secrets, a dead-on-arrival order-creation path, and no compensation between payment/persistence/publish
insights.detail: 1) Secrets are committed and live: PAYMENT_API_SECRET (apps/api/app/config.py:9) and the default DATABASE_URL password (apps/api/app/config.py:6, docker-compose.yml:8) are in git and actively used — rotate them first, it's the fastest real compromise. 2) POST /orders cannot succeed as written: the router always builds an Order with an empty lines list (apps/api/app/routers/orders.py:23-27), and OrderService.create unconditionally rejects orders with no lines (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:26-27) — the core feature of the API is broken. 3) Order creation charges Stripe, then saves to Postgres, then publishes to Kafka in-process with no error handling or outbox (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:28-39); a failure after the charge leaves a customer billed with no order record or no fulfilment ever triggered. Fix order: rotate the secrets immediately (near-zero effort, real exposure), then fix the order-creation bug (nothing works without it), then add a resilient publish/outbox path.

insights.title: Non-obvious conventions: shared's import name differs from its package name, DEBUG isn't env-driven, and there's a real import cycle
insights.detail: acme-shared is declared and installed as 'acme-shared' (packages/shared/pyproject.toml:2) but imported as `shared` (e.g. apps/api/app/routers/orders.py:5) — that mismatch is exactly why the scanner flags apps/api/pyproject.toml's acme-shared dependency as 'unused': it's actually used everywhere. DEBUG mode is a hardcoded Python literal (apps/api/app/config.py:5), not read from an environment variable, so the Dockerfile's ENV DEBUG=1 (apps/api/Dockerfile:5) is a no-op — don't expect changing it to do anything. The controller/service/repository layers in acme-api form a real dependency cycle (app -> app/repositories -> app/routers -> app/services -> app, per section 3 of AI-REPORT.md), so new code should avoid adding further cross-layer imports. Finally, there are no test files anywhere in the repo (test_file_ratio 0.0, AI-REPORT.md section 1), so the CI 'test' job runs against no tests.

insights.title: Stripe, PostgreSQL and Kafka are single points of failure for order creation; the shipping API currently is not
insights.detail: Stripe down: order creation fails outright since Charge.create runs before anything is persisted (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:28-30) — no half-written state, but zero orders can be created. PostgreSQL down: every order read/write fails (apps/api/app/repositories/order_repository.py:12,17), with no fallback store. Kafka down: publish() (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:35-39) runs after the Stripe charge and the Postgres save with no try/except, so a broker outage at that point leaves a paid, persisted order that the worker will never hear about — nothing retries it. Redis down: the order-status cache.set call (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:31) would raise after payment and persistence already succeeded, for the same reason. AWS S3 down: only apps/worker/worker/storage.py:11 (invoice storage) fails, so fulfilment stalls but the customer-facing API is unaffected. shipping.acme-logistics.example: request_shipment (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:41-42) is not called from anywhere, so its outage currently breaks nothing.

insights.title: shipping.acme-logistics.example is a real, coded integration point — but it's currently dead code
insights.detail: SHIPPING_API is a concrete configured URL (apps/api/app/config.py:10), not an incidental string, and it's consumed by a real method, OrderService.request_shipment, which actually issues an HTTPS POST to it (apps/api/app/services/order_service.py:41-42). However nothing in the repository calls request_shipment — it isn't wired into any router or task — so today the integration exists in code but has zero live traffic; it's a genuine but unused integration point rather than a leftover comment.
